On the third day the fog lifted and the archipelago appeared, a scattering of green islands on a pewter sea. The captain, a phlegmatic Scot who had sailed these waters for thirty years, pointed out the reefs with the stem of his pipe and named each island as if introducing old acquaintances. Gulls wheeled above the mast, raucous and insatiable. The passengers, emboldened by the sunshine, emerged from their cabins pale and blinking, like creatures released from hibernation, and lined the rail to watch a pod of dolphins cavort in the bow wave. Even the curmudgeonly professor, who had complained about everything since they left port, was seen to smile. The expedition reached the escarpment at dusk, and the cartographer, a taciturn woman with an encyclopaedic memory for coastlines, unrolled her vellum maps beside the fire. Nobody spoke. The guide, whose garrulous stories had enlivened the long march, now sat in a lugubrious silence, whittling a stick into something that resembled a heron.
